sar.narrative: This report details an organized online micro-billing fraud scheme affecting cardholder C00348 on card account C00348-K1, as well as 19 additional customer accounts across the institution. Between January 7, 2017, and January 28, 2017, card C00348-K1 was subjected to six unauthorized online micro-authorizations in product category C totaling $23.17, with individual transaction amounts ranging from $2.10 to $5.08. The unauthorized transactions (IDs 3660245 through 3660250) were conducted via the online channel and associated with billing regions 325 and 264 without captured device identifiers. On January 28, 2017, customer C00348 notified the institution that they did not authorize transaction 3660250 or the associated activity. Prior account history confirmed that cardholder C00348 maintained an established baseline of in-person retail transactions, with zero historical activity in product category C. Graph intelligence revealed that 19 peer cards across 19 distinct customers—including C12975-K2, C05083-K1, and C01326-K2—experienced the identical micro-authorization pattern during January 2017. Furthermore, the unauthorized charges across peer cards exhibited sequential transaction numbering clustered between 3660174 and 3660349, demonstrating a coordinated automated micro-billing scheme. The transactions were spaced across days and weeks at low dollar values, systematically evading single-transaction fraud score thresholds and standard velocity rules. Card C00348-K1 has been blocked with total identified exposure of $23.17, connected cards have been flagged for monitoring, and this report is submitted to document the coordinated abuse.

Things to know. - **A risk score is a reason to look.** Never a verdict. - **Half the cases are legitimate.** Many look suspicious. An agent that blocks everything scores badly. - **The known patterns are not the only ones.** Some activity in this data fits none of the five. Noticing it and describing it in your own words is scored. - **Devices and regions connect people.** A device profile or a billing region shared across many cards in a short window is worth a look. Some cases can only be solved by asking what happened on *other* cards. - **The V, C, D, M and numeric id columns are real model features with no names.** You may use them as signals. Say so in your evidence rather than pretending to know what V127 means. - **Customer and analyst replies are not provided.** If your agent asks the customer or requests step-up authentication, simulate the response in your own system and record what you assumed in `evidence_requests`.

passages.section: Section 3a. A case is not a report
passages.text: Section 3a. A case is not a report. Two different things, and the agent produces both. **A case** (`CREATE_CASE`) is the bank's internal record of an investigation. Open one whenever fraud probability reaches 0.30, whenever you request evidence, or whenever a customer disputes a charge. A case can be closed as fraud or as legitimate. It can be updated when new evidence arrives. It should be written into the graph so later investigations can find it: a case that names a merchant or a device becomes evidence for the next analyst. **A suspicious activity report** (`FILE_REPORT`) is a regulatory filing sent outside the bank. File one when fraud is confirmed or strongly suspected **and** at least one of these holds: exposure exceeds $1,000; the activity connects to a shared device profile, a shared region cluster, or another customer's fraud; the pattern is coordinated or undocumented (rule R9). A report always has a case behind it. Most cases never need a report. The report narrative must stand on its own: who, what, when, where, how, and why it is suspicious. Deciding correctly between ""case only"" and ""case plus report"" is part of the next-best-action score.

Rule R6: Shared origin. When several cards show fraud from the same device profile, the same billing region, or the same recipient email in one window, name the shared element, recommend `CREATE_CASE` and `FILE_REPORT`, and `MONITOR_CONNECTED_CARDS` for every card that shares it.

19 other cards (19 other customers) newly show the same signature in the 30 days to the alert - 3+ online authorisations under $10, on a card that had not made such charges before - against 7 and 4 in the same window one and two months earlier: C12975-K2, C05083-K1, C01326-K2, C04528-K1, C09471-K2, C13290-K1, C00129-K1, C12223-K1, C04105-K2, C12030-K1, C11332-K1, C09582-K1.

Card C00348-K1 experienced an anomalous run of 6 online micro-authorizations under $10 in product C between 2017-01-07 and 2017-01-28 totaling $23.17, departing completely from the cardholder's baseline of in-person retail purchases.

A scheme peers query identified 19 peer cards across 19 customers exhibiting the identical anomalous pattern of 3+ online micro-authorizations under $10 in product C during January 2017, with tightly clustered sequential transaction IDs (3660174 to 3660349), establishing a coordinated cross-customer scheme.

Prior closed cases CC-3841 and CC-4086 confirm that structured online authorization activity designed to circumvent automated threshold detection across multiple customer accounts is classified as confirmed fraud under the undocumented pattern (Rule R9).

Flagged transaction 3660250 produced a very low model score of 0.001 (historical fraud rate 0.0063) and legacy risk score of 0.04, reflecting typical model baselines for isolated micro-dollar authorizations lacking device anomalies.
Billing region 264 shows a low hot-share of 0.0022 and lift of 0.12 relative to baseline across 905 transactions in the 7-day window, indicating no localized geographic fraud concentration.

report.summary: Customer C00348 reported unauthorized activity on card C00348-K1 regarding online transaction 3660250 ($4.05, product C). An investigation identified a sequence of six online micro-authorizations in product category C between January 7 and January 28, 2017, totaling $23.17, which completely departed from the cardholder's baseline of in-person retail spending. Graph analysis linked the activity to an automated micro-billing scheme spanning 19 additional customer cards with sequential transaction IDs between 3660174 and 3660349. Based on decisive evidence of coordinated cross-customer abuse fitting undocumented pattern R9, card C00348-K1 was blocked, connected cards were placed on monitoring, and a regulatory report was authorized.
report.stop_reason: The investigation ended pursuant to policy section 6 because decisive fraud probability (0.934) was reached based on two independent categories of evidence: a direct customer dispute corroborated by an abrupt cardholder behavioral shift, and strong cross-card graph links showing an identical micro-authorization scheme across 19 peer cards. Under policy section 6, further inquiry was unnecessary as additional steps would not change the decision to block the card and file a regulatory report.
report.sar_narrative: This report details an organized online micro-billing fraud scheme affecting cardholder C00348 on card account C00348-K1, as well as 19 additional customer accounts across the institution. Between January 7, 2017, and January 28, 2017, card C00348-K1 was subjected to six unauthorized online micro-authorizations in product category C totaling $23.17, with individual transaction amounts ranging from $2.10 to $5.08. The unauthorized transactions (IDs 3660245 through 3660250) were conducted via the online channel and associated with billing regions 325 and 264 without captured device identifiers. On January 28, 2017, customer C00348 notified the institution that they did not authorize transaction 3660250 or the associated activity. Prior account history confirmed that cardholder C00348 maintained an established baseline of in-person retail transactions, with zero historical activity in product category C. Graph intelligence revealed that 19 peer cards across 19 distinct customers—including C12975-K2, C05083-K1, and C01326-K2—experienced the identical micro-authorization pattern during January 2017. Furthermore, the unauthorized charges across peer cards exhibited sequential transaction numbering clustered between 3660174 and 3660349, demonstrating a coordinated automated micro-billing scheme. The transactions were spaced across days and weeks at low dollar values, systematically evading single-transaction fraud score thresholds and standard velocity rules. Card C00348-K1 has been blocked with total identified exposure of $23.17, connected cards have been flagged for monitoring, and this report is submitted to document the coordinated abuse.
